cpr1x: Tap firmly and shout. No response, not breathing normally? Move to the next step.
cpr2x: Call 144 (ambulance) before anything else. Put the call on speaker and lay the phone down.
cpr3x: Lay the person flat on their back, on a firm surface. Kneel beside their chest.
cpr4x: Two hands, heel of palm on the center of the chest, fingers interlocked, arms straight.
cpr5x: Push hard and fast, about 5–6 cm deep, at roughly 100–120 per minute — the tempo of a fast heartbeat. Let the chest fully rise between pushes.
cpr6x: Continue compressions without stopping until paramedics arrive or the person starts breathing normally. Swap with someone else every ~2 minutes if you can, without pausing compressions for long.
cpr7x: If a defibrillator (AED) is nearby, send someone for it now — turn it on and follow its voice prompts alongside compressions.

safety_roof_1T: Fall protection is mandatory above 2–3 m
safety_roof_1X: Any roof edge with a drop of more than 2 m (BauAV) generally needs protection; SUVA's own guidance sets the practical threshold at 3 m depending on roof pitch. Collective protection (scaffolding, guardrails, safety nets) always takes priority over personal gear like a harness.
safety_roof_2X: Above roughly 25–30° pitch a roofer's protection wall (Dachdeckerschutzwand) is required; above 60° a mobile elevating platform or equivalent is typically needed instead of a harness alone.
safety_roof_3X: Roof lights and openings aren't reliably break-proof — they need their own additional securing (safety glass, grille, netting), not just general edge protection.
safety_roof_4X: Personal fall-arrest gear (PSAgA) may only be used when collective protection genuinely isn't possible, and requires at least basic training in anchor points and use.
safety_roof_5X: Protection is also required against tools or material falling from the roof onto people below, not just against people falling.
safety_metal_1T: Fume extraction when welding or grinding
safety_metal_1X: Welding and cutting metal must use extraction or ventilation plus the required respirator — welding fume is a recognised health hazard, and some fumes carry a cancer risk.
safety_metal_2T: Hands and eyes are the most common injuries
safety_metal_2X: Cut-resistant gloves, welding-rated eyewear, and spark/UV-resistant welder's clothing are minimum kit — fingers, hands and eyes account for most metalwork injuries.
safety_metal_3X: Assembling steel frames, glass facade elements, or roof flashing at height follows the same fall-protection rules as any other trade — secure yourself and only stand on load-bearing surfaces.
safety_metal_4T: Only trained staff run cranes or rig loads
safety_metal_4X: Craning and rigging loads (including glass and frame elements) requires trained personnel and properly rated lifting gear.
safety_metal_5T: Check for asbestos on pre-1990 material
safety_metal_5X: Before welding, cutting, or grinding older material, confirm whether it contains asbestos and take the required precautions if so.
safety_formwork_1T: Edge protection required above 2 m since 2025
safety_formwork_1X: As of 1 January 2025, fall protection is mandatory on slab/deck formwork work above 2 m (the earlier practical exception sat at 3 m). Collective protection — nets, guardrails — is preferred over a harness alone.
safety_formwork_2T: Use a platform ladder above 1 m
safety_formwork_2X: When fitting props, pour platforms, or edge-protection parts above 1 m, use a podium/platform ladder or similar aid rather than working freestanding.
safety_formwork_3T: Fit elements while they're lying flat
safety_formwork_3X: Attach props, pour platforms and side-protection parts to formwork panels while they're still on the ground where possible, and only release the crane sling once the element is fully secured.
safety_formwork_4X: Formwork systems assembled from below (element or beam-grid systems) avoid working at height entirely and are inherently safer than conventional top-down formwork.
safety_ground_1T: Trenches over 1.5 m need shoring or sloping
safety_ground_1X: Any trench, shaft, or excavation deeper than 1.5 m must be shored, sloped, or otherwise secured (BauAV) — this is the threshold SUVA cites, and fatal accidents have happened at depths as shallow as 1.2 m.
safety_ground_2T: Know what's underground before you dig
safety_ground_2X: Existing gas, water, power, or other buried lines must be located and marked before excavation starts.
safety_ground_3T: Keep vehicles and material back from the edge
safety_ground_3X: A safety strip of at least 0.6 m must stay clear at the top edge on both sides, and slopes must never be additionally loaded by vehicles, machinery, or material stockpiles.
safety_ground_4X: Hard hats are required in trenches and pits, and anywhere near excavators or heavy earthmoving machinery.
safety_ground_5T: Steep or deep slopes need an engineer's sign-off
safety_ground_5X: Slopes steeper than roughly 45–63° (depending on soil type), deeper than 4 m, or subject to extra load, water, or vibration require a formal stability assessment by a qualified engineer or geotechnician.
